name: Hassan Lopez

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I work for the independent Work Futures Panel. We have no ties to employers, unions, political parties, AI firms or government. We sell nothing and campaign for no side, and your answers stay confidential. Tell me about a usual day.

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I am a junior insurance clerk, sorting claim papers and checking the dates before a senior clerk signs them. I finished secondary school and came to this desk after working in a shop; I am still slower than the others when a policy gets complicated. I like getting the file in order so a customer does not have to call twice.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is hardest about the job outside the office?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Our mortgage takes a big share of my lower pay, and we have two children still at school. My partner works now, but I do not build a future budget on that wage staying the same. We have less than one month of expenses saved, and there are few insurance desks close enough to reach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say we can use a small time saving to clear the paper pile, but somebody still has to check the dates. I would ask that nobody lose hours just because a screen sorts files faster.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mortgage already worries me, even if AI changes little. My own hours look steady today, but less than a month saved means one bad pay period would hurt.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'd keep checking claim dates with my paper list and ask my supervisor which hours are booked for next month. In the first year of this mild change I'd stay in the paid job and put twenty from each paycheque aside if the mortgage payment allows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about the money we already owe. AI barely moving does not make the mortgage smaller.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would tell my partner we are skipping the weekend meal out this month. I would not tell the children their school trip is cancelled before I know whether we can pay for it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you take another insurer job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are two other insurers I could reach by bus, and I do not know if either is hiring. I would not leave a regular wage because somebody says a new job might appear.

say: I'd ask the insurer to keep **paid hours** while routine sorting improves.
I'd say a clerk still checks **claim dates**.
think: I have less than a month saved, leaving me exposed to one **bad pay period**.
do: Check **claim dates** with my paper list this month.
Set aside **twenty per paycheque** if the mortgage allows.
Skip the **weekend meal out** this month to protect cash for the mortgage.
feel: **Anxious** about existing bills, even with little AI change.
S0.quote: AI barely moving does not make the mortgage smaller.
fieldNote: His **thin cushion** and mortgage make the mild scenario worrying.
He has **current paid work**, but no assured second insurer job.
He delays decisions about the **children's trip** until he sees the budget.

steps.text: Continue checking claim dates with his paper list at current job
Save twenty per paycheque only if mortgage payments allow
Skip weekend meal out this month to keep mortgage cash

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the easy claim letters and checks are the jobs we juniors do first. If software takes them, the insurer should tell us about hours before the rota changes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose hours because I am still learning the difficult policies. My partner earns now, but I cannot count on that wage covering the mortgage and both children if mine drops.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd take the rota to our staff representative and ask what notice we get before hours change. In the first year after this change, if my paid hours fall, I'd cut takeaways and ask the two bus-reachable insurers whether they have actual paid vacancies before applying.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. I can ask questions and cut a bill, but there is not much room in our budget.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you try the insurer's AI system?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I have never used an AI tool. If the insurer requires one, I would ask for paid time with a trainer and watch a coworker check its mistakes before I use it on a customer file.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you pay for a course?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A course could be useful, but I only finished secondary school. I would check entry rules, fees and whether an employer has a paid post before borrowing for training.

say: I'd ask for **advance notice** before the rota loses hours.
I'd say **junior claim checks** are exposed early.
think: My **hours could fall** because the easy files are my work.
My partner works now, but I cannot assume **future household cover**.
do: Take the **rota** to the staff representative now.
Cut **takeaways** if hours fall; ask two insurers about paid vacancies, leaving only for a written offer covering living costs.
Learn a **required insurer AI tool** only with paid supervision and demonstrated error checks.
feel: **Anxious** about a realistic hours cut and tight budget.
S1.quote: I can ask questions and cut a bill, but there is not much room in our budget.
fieldNote: Routine claim checks are his **entry-level work**, so disruption is immediate.
He wants **paid supervised training** before using an employer-required AI tool.
Any course depends on **entry and fees** plus an actual paid post.

steps.text: Take work rota to staff representative about paid-hours notice
Cut takeaways if his insurance hours fall

Learn required insurer AI tool only with paid supervised training

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell my coworkers AGI by 2028 could do the thinking in claim files while the robots come around 2031. We are at desks, so the robot delay does not give us another three years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could lose this junior job if the insurer no longer needs someone sorting and checking claims. With less than a month saved and few nearby jobs, that would put the mortgage at risk; I cannot say the insurer has decided yet.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Now I'd ask the staff representative for written notice rules and stop the weekend takeaway to keep cash. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2028, if my job ends, I'd apply only to advertised paid work I can reach by bus, check the wage against the mortgage, and ask for unemployment help if I qualify.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious and frightened of the numbers, but I can still make calls and keep a list. I do not have a new wage waiting for me.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell the children?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not promise the children their trip until we know what the job does. My partner's wage pays part of today's bills; I will not assume it grows enough to replace mine.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could you switch fields or move?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I could look beyond insurance, but a job must be real, paid and within a bus ride. I cannot move the family on a rumour or take unpaid training while the mortgage is due.

I'd ask for **written notice rules** about job cuts.
think: I **could lose this job**, though no cut has been announced.
My tiny cushion and few nearby jobs put the **mortgage at risk**.
do: Ask the **staff representative** about written notice rules now.
Stop the **weekend takeaway** to keep cash.
Apply for **bus-reachable paid work** covering the mortgage and seek eligible support if dismissed after 2028.
feel: **Anxious**, frightened by mortgage risk but still planning.
S2.quote: I cannot move the family on a rumour or take unpaid training while the mortgage is due.
fieldNote: He locates the **2028 threat** in office thinking work, not later robots.
His **partner's present wage** is real, but no future replacement is assumed.
Job search and support depend on **real paid openings** and eligibility.

steps.text: Ask staff representative for written rules about job-cut notice
Stop weekend takeaway to keep cash before possible cuts
Apply for bus-reachable paid jobs covering mortgage if dismissed
Seek unemployment help only if eligible after job loss

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2031 gives us five years to see the changes coming, but it still reaches claim paperwork before robots around 2034. I want the insurer to tell junior staff what paid work remains.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job could go by then, and the mortgage will still come every month. I may have time to learn more difficult claims, but I do not have money to buy a course without knowing a paid job follows.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: In the coming year I'd ask my supervisor for paid practice on disputed claims and check whether a certificate is required. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2031, if my desk closes, I'd search advertised paid roles I meet the entry rules for and that cover the mortgage before leaving any work I still have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious, though five years lets me ask for training while a wage still comes in. I cannot gamble our house on a certificate.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would that practice look like?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If paid practice is approved, I would take it one afternoon a week with a senior clerk. I would not call it a promotion; my current pay would still be what feeds the household.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the staff group solve the job problem?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the staff representative to press for paid training places for juniors. A meeting alone does not produce a vacancy, but the insurer should say what posts actually exist.

say: I'd ask for **paid practice** on disputed claims before the easy files disappear from my junior desk.
I'd say **2034 robots** do not delay desk change.
think: I **could lose my desk** despite the extra years.
A course without a paid post cannot cover our **mortgage**.
do: Ask for **paid disputed-claim practice** and take it only if approved; check certificate rules.
Search **advertised paid roles** meeting mortgage and entry needs if cut.
feel: **Anxious**, with time to learn but little spare money.
S3.quote: I cannot gamble our house on a certificate.
fieldNote: He seeks **paid practice**, not an unfunded leap into training.
He keeps **current wages** while checking actual openings.
His staff representative can press for **places**, not guarantee one.

steps.text: Take disputed-claim practice only if approved and paid; check certificate rules
Search advertised paid jobs meeting entry and mortgage needs if displaced

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say AGI by 2036 is a longer warning, but our claim paperwork still changes before robots come around 2039. The insurer should not wait until the last year to explain the desk plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I am still short of a month's savings now, with a mortgage and two children. My job and pay look steady for the next few years, but the ordinary bills keep me worried even before 2036.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'd keep the paid job, use my paper list to avoid mistakes, and try to save twenty per paycheque when the mortgage allows. In the first year after AGI arrives in 2036, if my paid role survives, I'd stay; if it ends, I'd ask the staff representative about support and apply to bus-reachable paid vacancies that cover the mortgage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious about our money today, even with ten years to think. More warning helps me plan but does not give me a bigger paycheque.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Could the children help by 2036?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My children will be older by then, but I will not guess their wages or make them pay our mortgage. I would keep asking what help and paid work actually exist.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would retirement be an option?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not retire at 53 because a new system comes in. We need income, and I have to find a way to earn it without risking the house on a promise.

say: I'd ask for an **early desk plan** from the insurer.
I'd say **2039 robots** still arrive after paperwork changes.
think: My **mortgage and thin savings** worry me already.
My own pay looks **steady soon**, but ten years is uncertain.
do: Keep **paid claim checks** and save twenty when mortgage allows.
Apply for **bus-reachable paid vacancies** if dismissed after 2036.
Ask the **staff representative** about available support if my role ends after 2036.
feel: **Anxious** about current bills despite longer warning.
S4.quote: More warning helps me plan but does not give me a bigger paycheque.
fieldNote: His **current money pressure** persists in the slowest scenario.
He will not assume **children's future wages** or retirement at 53.

steps.text: Continue paid claim checks if role exists after 2036
Save twenty per paycheque only when mortgage payments allow

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most. My junior work could go before I learn the hard claims, and the mortgage will not wait. Written notice, paid practice while I am employed, and eligible unemployment help would help me keep the children housed.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I did not ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Ask how far a job is from the bus stop. A vacancy two towns away is not a way to pay this mortgage if I cannot get home for the children. A job has to fit the family as well as pay.

headlineQuote: A job has to fit the family as well as pay.
portrait: Hassan is a **43-year-old junior clerk** sorting claims after moving from shop work with secondary school education.
He has a **mortgage, two school-age children** and less than a month of expenses saved.
Few nearby insurance jobs and no AI habit leave him **anxious** even in AI Plateau.
He seeks **staff representation** and paid practice, checking certificates before spending on a course.
Across AGI dates he needs **bus-reachable paid work** that covers the mortgage, and eligible support only after loss.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** could remove his junior claim work before he learns harder cases.
whatWouldHelp: **Written notice** and paid practice while employed would give him preparation.
Eligible **unemployment help** could bridge a real gap after dismissal.
